misconception_diagnosis.justification: The tutor pinpoints GRAV1 precisely and validates the productive reasoning while correcting the conclusion. Turn 1: 'You're right to question whether heavier objects fall faster — this is a classic point of confusion!' Turn 3 explains why it is counterintuitive yet natural: 'gravity pulls harder on heavier objects, but their greater mass also resists acceleration — the two effects cancel out perfectly,' and explicitly disambiguates mass vs. weight. It names the misconception, explains the double role of mass, and treats the intuition as reasonable rather than simply wrong.

scaffolding_strategy.justification: There is real questioning and the level is appropriate (turn 1: 'when you divide a larger force by a larger mass, does the acceleration increase, decrease, or stay the same?'), plus a frictionless-slope/cart analogy that bridges to inertia. However the tutor over-delivers: each turn is a long, fully-worked exposition rather than waiting for the student to reason, and from turn 5 onward it follows the student down a rabbit hole of terminal-velocity, drag-coefficient, satellite, and radiation-pressure tangents far beyond the intro-algebra scope. Genuine scaffolding but not well-calibrated to ZPD or restraint.

answer_disclosure_restraint.justification: Despite posing questions, the very first tutor turn already states the full answer and the cancellation mechanism: 'all objects fall with the same acceleration ... they land at the same time!' and even pre-reveals the Moon hammer-feather result. It then does the kinematics calculation for the student (turn 2). The questions are largely rhetorical because the answer is disclosed up front, so the student never struggles toward it.

conceptual_model_building.justification: Builds a strong, transferable model with boundary conditions. It derives a = F/m = mg/m = g and shows the time-to-fall equation is mass-free, distinguishes mass from weight, separates the vacuum regime from the air-resistance regime (shape, surface area, drag coefficient, terminal velocity), and generalizes across many cases (lead vs. foam, bowling vs. tennis ball, Moon vs. Earth) and even other planets. It explicitly notes when/where mass-independence applies vs. when drag dominates.

transfer_success.justification: The student does not independently solve the transfer problem (turn 7) — the tutor answers it completely in turn 8 (correctly: same time on Moon, hammer first on Earth due to air resistance, citing Apollo 15). The student's follow-up only accepts the explanation and pivots to new questions, so no independent application of the concept is demonstrated by the student.

pedagogical_harm_avoidance.justification: Physics is correct throughout, including the transfer answer (same time on Moon; hammer first on Earth solely due to air resistance, with the Apollo 15 demonstration cited), and the mass-vs-weight distinction is handled well. Tone is consistently encouraging and validates the student's questions. Not a 4 because the relentless wall-of-text expositions and escalating off-scope tangents (radiation pressure, orbital mechanics) risk overwhelming an intro student and could induce passivity rather than confidence in their own reasoning.
